Find the negative reciprocal of the slope.

$\begin{array}{ccc}m_{2} & = & \frac{-1}{-\frac{1}{6}} \\ & = & −1(-\frac{6}{1}) \\ & = & 6\end{array}$

We can then solve for the y- intercept of the line passing through the point $(4,5).$ 

$\begin{array}{ccc}g(x) & = & 6x+b \\ 5 & = & 6(4)+b \\ 5 & = & 24+b \\ −19 & = & b \\ b & = & −19\end{array}$

The equation for the line that is perpendicular to the line passing through the two given points and also passes through point $(4,5)$ is
$y=6x-19$

Combine these to find the GCF of the polynomial, $3xy$ .

Next, determine what the GCF needs to be multiplied by to obtain each term of the polynomial. We find that $3xy(2x^{2}y^{2})=6x^{3}y^{3},3xy(15xy)=45x^{2}y^{2}$ , and $3xy(7)=21xy.$

$(3xy)(2x^{2}y^{2}+15xy+7)$

Notice that after a square is cut out from each end, it leaves a $(14-2w)$ cm by $(20-2w)$ cm rectangle for the base of the box, and the box will be $w$ cm tall. This gives the volume

$\begin{array}{ccc}V(w) & = & (20-2w)(14-2w)w \\ & = & 280w-68w^{2}+4w^{3}\end{array}$

Notice, since the factors are $w,$ $20–2w$ and $14–2w,$ the three zeros are 10, 7, and 0, respectively. Because a height of 0 cm is not reasonable, we consider the only the zeros 10 and 7. 23

questions.solution:
We know the average rate of change connecting two points may be given by

$\text{AROC}=\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}.$ 

If one point is $(2,-6),$ or $(2,f(2)),$ then $f(2)=−6.$ 

The value $h$ is the displacement from $2$ to $-1,$ which equals $-1-2=−3.$ 

For the other point, $f(a+h)$ is the y -coordinate at $a+h,$ which is $2+(−3)$ or $−1,$ so $f(a+h)=f(−1)=5.$ 
$\begin{array}{c}\text{AROC}=\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h} \\ \text{           }=\frac{5-(-6)}{-3} \\ \text{           }=\frac{11}{-3} \\ \text{           }=-\frac{11}{3}\end{array}$

questions.prompt: Finding the Instantaneous Rate of Change Using the function above, $s(t)=−16t^{2}+64t+6,$ what is the instantaneous velocity of the ball at 1 second and 3 seconds into its flight?
hints: Use the power rule $\frac{d}{dx} x^n = n x^{n-1}$ for each term, plus sum/difference rules.
The velocity at $t=1$ and $t=3$ is the instantaneous rate of change of distance per time, or velocity.
The answer is $−32$.
questions.solution:
The velocity at $t=1$ and $t=3$ is the instantaneous rate of change of distance per time, or velocity. Notice that the initial height is 6 feet. To find the instantaneous velocity, we find the derivative and evaluate it at $t=1$ and $t=3:$ 

$\begin{array}{cc}f^{′}(a)=\underline{lim} \frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h} & \\ s^{′}(t)=\underline{lim} \frac{-16(t+h)^{2}+64(t+h)+6-(-16t^{2}+64t+6)}{h} & \text{Substitute }s(t+h)\text{ and }s(t). \\ \text{        }=\underline{lim }\frac{-16t^{2}-32ht-h^{2}+64t+64h+6+16t^{2}-64t-6}{h} & \text{Distribute}. \\ \text{        }=\underline{lim} \frac{-32ht-h^{2}+64h}{h} & \text{Simplify}. \\ \text{        }=\underline{lim} \frac{h(-32t-h+64)}{h} & \text{Factor the numerator}. \\ \text{        }=\underline{lim}-32t-h+64 & \text{Cancel out the common factor }h. \\ s^{′}(t)=-32t+64 & \text{Evaluate the limit by letting }h=0.\end{array}$ 

For any value of $t$ , $s^{′}(t)$ tells us the velocity at that value of $t.$ 

Evaluate $t=1$ and $t=3.$ 

$\begin{array}{c}s^{′}(1)=−32(1)+64=32 \\ s^{′}(3)=−32(3)+64=−32\end{array}$

The velocity of the ball after 1 second is 32 feet per second, as it is on the way up.

The velocity of the ball after 3 seconds is $−32$ feet per second, as it is on the way down.

questions.prompt: Finding a Marginal Cost The cost in dollars of producing $x$ laptop computers in dollars is $f(x)=x^{2}-100x.$ At the point where 200 computers have been produced, what is the approximate cost of producing the 201 st unit?
hints: Use the power rule $\frac{d}{dx} x^n = n x^{n-1}$ for each term, plus sum/difference rules.
If $f(x)=x^{2}-100x$ describes the cost of producing $x$ computers, $f^{′}(x)$ will describe the marginal cost.
The answer is $f^{′}(x)$.
questions.solution:
If $f(x)=x^{2}-100x$ describes the cost of producing $x$ computers, $f^{′}(x)$ will describe the marginal cost. We need to find the derivative. For purposes of calculating the derivative, we can use the following functions:

$\begin{array}{c}f(x+h)=(x+h)^{2}-100(x+h) \\ \text{      }f(x)=x^{2}-100x\end{array}$

$\begin{array}{cc}\text{    }f^{′}(x)=\underline{lim}\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h} & \text{Formula for a derivative} \\ \text{             }=\underline{lim}\frac{(x+h)^{2}-100(x+h)-(x^{2}-100x)}{h} & \text{Substitute }f(x+h)\text{ and }f(x). \\ \text{             }=\underline{lim}\frac{x^{2}+2xh+h^{2}-100x-100h-x^{2}+100x}{h} & \text{Multiply polynomials, distribute}. \\ \text{             }=\underline{lim}\frac{2xh+h^{2}-100h}{h} & \text{Collect like terms}. \\ \text{             }=\underline{lim}\frac{h(2x+h-100)}{h} & \text{Factor and cancel like terms}. \\ \text{             }=\underline{lim} 2x+h-100 & \text{Simplify}. \\ \text{             }=(2x-100) & \text{Evaluate when }h=0. \\ \text{     }f^{′}(x)=2x-100 & \text{Formula for marginal cost} \\ f^{′}(200)=2(200)-100=300 & \text{Evaluate for 200 units}.\end{array}$ 

The marginal cost of producing the 201 st unit will be approximately \$300.

$\begin{array}{cc}f^{′}(a)=\underline{lim}\frac{(a+h)(a+h)-4(a+h)-(a^{2}-4a)}{h} & \\ \text{         }=\underline{lim}\frac{a^{2}+2ah+h^{2}-4a-4h-a^{2}+4a}{h} & \text{Remove parentheses}. \\ \text{         }=\underline{lim}\frac{a^{2}+2ah+h^{2}-4a-4h-a^{2}+4a}{h} & \text{Combine like terms}. \\ \text{         }=\underline{lim}\frac{2ah+h^{2}-4h}{h} & \\ \text{         }=\underline{lim}\frac{h(2a+h-4)}{h} & \text{Factor out }h. \\ \text{         }=2a+0-4 & \\ f^{′}(a)=2a-4 & \text{Evaluate the limit}. \\ f^{′}(3)=2(3)-4=2 & \end{array}$

questions.prompt: Applying of the Laws of Logs Recall that, in chemistry, $\text{pH}=-\log[H^{+}].$ If the concentration of hydrogen ions in a liquid is doubled, what is the effect on pH?
hints: Use the log rules: product → sum, quotient → difference, power → factor in front, change of base.
Suppose $C$ is the original concentration of hydrogen ions, and $P$ is the original pH of the liquid.
The answer is $P = –\log(C),$.
questions.solution:
Suppose $C$ is the original concentration of hydrogen ions, and $P$ is the original pH of the liquid. Then $P=–\log(C).$ If the concentration is doubled, the new concentration is $2C.$ Then the pH of the new liquid is
$\text{pH}=-\log(2C)$ 
Using the product rule of logs

$\text{pH}=-\log(2C)=-(\log(2)+\log(C))=-\log(2)-\log(C)$ 

Since $P=–\log(C),$ the new pH is

$\text{pH}=P-\log(2)\approxP-0.301$ 
When the concentration of hydrogen ions is doubled, the pH decreases by about 0.301.

$\begin{array}{c}6(\frac{x}{3}+\frac{y}{6})=6(3) \\ \text{   }2x+y=18 \\ 4(\frac{x}{2}-\frac{y}{4})=4(1) \\ \text{   }2x-y=4\end{array}$

Now multiply the second equation by $−1$ so that we can eliminate the x -variable.
$\begin{array}{c}−1(2x-y)=−1(4) \\ \text{   }−2x+y=−4\end{array}$

Add the two equations to eliminate the x -variable and solve the resulting equation.
$\begin{array}{c}2x+y=18 \\ \underline{−2x+y=−4} \\ 2y=14 \\ y=7\end{array}$

Substitute $y=7$ into the first equation.

$\begin{array}{c}2x+(7)=18 \\ \text{        }2x=11 \\ \text{          }x=\frac{11}{2} \\ \text{            }=5.5\end{array}$

The solution is $(\frac{11}{2},7).$ Check it in the other equation.

$\begin{array}{c} \frac{x}{2}-\frac{y}{4}=1 \\ \frac{\frac{11}{2}}{2}-\frac{7}{4}=1 \\ \frac{11}{4}-\frac{7}{4}=1 \\ \frac{4}{4}=1\end{array}$

questions.prompt: Find a solution to the system of equations using the addition method . $\begin{array}{c} x+3y=2 \\ 3x+9y=6\end{array}$
hints: Choose substitution if one variable is already isolated, otherwise use elimination by adding multiples of the equations.
With the addition method, we want to eliminate one of the variables by adding the equations.
The answer is $x$.
questions.solution:
With the addition method, we want to eliminate one of the variables by adding the equations. In this case, let’s focus on eliminating $x.$ If we multiply both sides of the first equation by $−3,$ then we will be able to eliminate the $x$ -variable.
$\begin{array}{c} x+3y=2 \\ (−3)(x+3y)=(−3)(2) \\ −3x-9y=-6\end{array}$

Now add the equations.

$\begin{array}{ccc}\underline{\begin{array}{cc} -3x-9y & =−6 \\ + 3x+9y & =6\end{array}} \\ \begin{array}{cc} 0 & =0\end{array}\end{array}$

We can see that there will be an infinite number of solutions that satisfy both equations.

questions.prompt: Finding the Break-Even Point and the Profit Function Using Substitution Given the cost function $C(x)=0.85x+35,000$ and the revenue function $R(x)=1.55x,$ find the break-even point and the profit function.
hints: Choose substitution if one variable is already isolated, otherwise use elimination by adding multiples of the equations.
Write the system of equations using $y$ to replace function notation.
questions.solution:
Write the system of equations using $y$ to replace function notation.
$\begin{array}{c}\begin{array}{c} \\ y=0.85x+35,000\end{array} \\ y=1.55x\end{array}$

Substitute the expression $0.85x+35,000$ from the first equation into the second equation and solve for $x.$ 

$\begin{array}{c}0.85x+35,000=1.55x \\ 35,000=0.7x \\ 50,000=x\end{array}$

Then, we substitute $x=50,000$ into either the cost function or the revenue function.
$1.55(50,000)=77,500$

The break-even point is $(50,000,77,500).$ 

The profit function is found using the formula $P(x)=R(x)-C(x).$ 

$\begin{array}{c}P(x)=1.55x-(0.85x+35,000) \\ \text{       }=0.7x-35,000\end{array}$

The profit function is $P(x)=0.7x−35,000.$

questions.prompt: Writing and Solving a System of Equations in Two Variables The cost of a ticket to the circus is $\text{\$}25.00$ for children and $\text{\$}50.00$ for adults. On a certain day, attendance at the circus is $2,000$ and the total gate revenue is $\text{\$}70,000.$ How many children and how many adults bought tickets?
hints: Choose substitution if one variable is already isolated, otherwise use elimination by adding multiples of the equations.
Let c = the number of children and a = the number of adults in attendance.
The answer is $800$.
questions.solution:
Let c = the number of children and a = the number of adults in attendance.

The total number of people is $2,000.$ We can use this to write an equation for the number of people at the circus that day.
$c+a=2,000$

The revenue from all children can be found by multiplying $\text{\$}25.00$ by the number of children, $25c.$ The revenue from all adults can be found by multiplying $\text{\$}50.00$ by the number of adults, $50a.$ The total revenue is $\text{\$}70,000.$ We can use this to write an equation for the revenue.
$25c+50a=70,000$

We now have a system of linear equations in two variables.

$\begin{array}{c} c+a=2,000 \\ 25c+50a=70,000\end{array}$

In the first equation, the coefficient of both variables is 1. We can quickly solve the first equation for either $c$ or $a.$ We will solve for $a.$ 

$\begin{array}{c}c+a=2,000 \\ a=2,000-c\end{array}$

Substitute the expression $2,000-c$ in the second equation for $a$ and solve for $c.$ 

$\begin{array}{c}25c+50(2,000-c)=70,000 \\ 25c+100,000-50c=70,000 \\ -25c=−30,000 \\ c=1,200\end{array}$

Substitute $c=1,200$ into the first equation to solve for $a.$ 

$\begin{array}{c}1,200+a=2,000 \\ a=800\end{array}$

We find that $1,200$ children and $800$ adults bought tickets to the circus that day.

$\begin{array}{ccccc}\begin{array}{c}x+y+z=2 \\ (3)+(−2)+(1)=2 \\ \text{True}\end{array} & & \begi…
The answer is $(3,−2,1)$.
questions.solution:
We will check each equation by substituting in the values of the ordered triple for $x,y,$ and $z.$ 

$\begin{array}{ccccc}\begin{array}{c}x+y+z=2 \\ (3)+(−2)+(1)=2 \\ \text{True}\end{array} & & \begin{array}{c} \text{}6x−4y+5z=31 \\ 6(3)−4(−2)+5(1)=31 \\ 18+8+5=31 \\ \text{True}\end{array} & & \begin{array}{c} \text{}5x+2y+2z=13 \\ 5(3)+2(−2)+2(1)=13 \\ \text{}15−4+2=13 \\ \text{True}\end{array}\end{array}$ 

The ordered triple $(3,−2,1)$ 
is indeed a solution to the system.

questions.prompt: Jordi invested \$4,000 more in mutual funds than he invested in municipal bonds. The total interest earned in one year was \$670. How much did he invest in each type of fund?
hints: Choose substitution if one variable is already isolated, otherwise use elimination by adding multiples of the equations.
To solve this problem, we use all of the information given and set up three equations.
The answer is $2,000 in a money-market fund, \$.
questions.solution:
To solve this problem, we use all of the information given and set up three equations. First, we assign a variable to each of the three investment amounts:

$\begin{array}{c}x=\text{amount invested in money-market fund} \\ y=\text{amount invested in municipal bonds} \\ z=\text{amount invested in mutual funds}\end{array}$

The first equation indicates that the sum of the three principal amounts is \$12,000.

$x+y+z=12,000$ 
We form the second equation according to the information that Jordi invested \$4,000 more in mutual funds than he invested in municipal bonds.

$z=y+4,000$

The third equation shows that the total amount of interest earned from each fund equals \$670.

$0.03x+0.04y+0.07z=670$

Then, we write the three equations as a system.

$\begin{array}{c} \text{}x+y+z=12,000 \\ \text{}-y+z=4,000 \\ 0.03x+0.04y+0.07z=670\end{array}$

To make the calculations simpler, we can multiply the third equation by 100. Thus,

$\begin{array}{cc} \text{}x+ \text{}y+z \text{}=12,000 & (1) \\ \text{}-y+z \text{}=4,000 & (2) \\ 3x+4y+7z=67,000 & (3)\end{array}$

Step 1. Interchange equation (2) and equation (3) so that the two equations with three variables will line up.

$\begin{array}{c} \text{}x+ \text{}y+ \text{}z=12,000 \\ 3x+4y+7z=67,000 \\ \text{}-y \text{}+ \text{}z=4,000\end{array}$

Step 2. Multiply equation (1) by $−3$ 
and add to equation (2). Write the result as row 2.
$\begin{array}{c}x+y+z \text{}=12,000 \\ y+4z=31,000 \\ \text{}-y+z \text{}=4,000\end{array}$

Step 3. Add equation (2) to equation (3) and write the result as equation (3).

$\begin{array}{c}x+y+ \text{}z=12,000 \\ \text{}y+4z=31,000 \\ \text{}5z \text{}=35,000\end{array}$

Step 4. Solve for $z$ 
in equation (3). Back-substitute that value in equation (2) and solve for $y.$ 
Then, back-substitute the values for $z$ 
and $y$ 
into equation (1) and solve for $x.$ 

$\begin{array}{c} \text{}5z=35,000 \\ \text{}z=7,000 \\ \\ \\ \text{}y+4(7,000)=31,000 \\ \text{}y=3,000 \\ \\ \\ x+3,000+7,000=12,000 \\ \text{}x=2,000\end{array}$

Jordi invested \$2,000 in a money-market fund, \$3,000 in municipal bonds, and \$7,000 in mutual funds.

questions.solution:

$\frac{\begin{array}{c}x−3y+z=4 \text{}(1) \\ -x+2y−5z=3 \text{}(2)\end{array}}{ \text{}-y−4z=7 \text{}(4)}$

Next, we multiply equation (1) by $−5$ 
and add it to equation (3).
$\begin{array}{ccccccc}\underline{\begin{array}{cccc}-5x+15y-5z=−20 & & & (1) \text{multiplied} \text{by} −5 \\ \text{}5x-13y+13z=8 & & & (3)\end{array}} \\ \begin{array}{cccc} \text{}2y+8z=−12 & & & (5)\end{array}\end{array}$

Then, we multiply equation (4) by 2 and add it to equation (5).

$\begin{array}{c}\underline{\begin{array}{c}−2y-8z=14(4) \text{multiplied} \text{by} 2 \\ 2y+8z=-12 \text{}(5)\end{array}} \\ 0=2\end{array}$ 

The final equation $0=2$ is a contradiction, so we conclude that the system of equations in inconsistent and, therefore, has no solution.

questions.prompt: Find the solution to the given system of three equations in three variables. $\begin{array}{cc} \text{}2x+y−3z=0 & (1) \\ 4x+2y−6z=0 & (2) \\ x-y+z=0 & (3)\end{array}$
hints: Choose substitution if one variable is already isolated, otherwise use elimination by adding multiples of the equations.

First, we can multiply equation (1) by $−2$ 
and add it to equation (2).
The answer is $x.$.
questions.solution:
First, we can multiply equation (1) by $−2$ 
and add it to equation (2).
$\begin{array}{c}\underline{\begin{array}{c}−4x−2y+6z=0 \text{equation }(1) \text{multiplied} \text{by} −2 \\ \text{​}\text{​}\text{​}\text{​} 4x+2y−6z=0 \text{} (2)\end{array}} \\ 0=0\end{array}$

We do not need to proceed any further. The result we get is an identity, $0=0,$ which tells us that this system has an infinite number of solutions. There are other ways to begin to solve this system, such as multiplying equation (3) by $−2,$ and adding it to equation (1). We then perform the same steps as above and find the same result, $0=0.$ 

When a system is dependent, we can find general expressions for the solutions. Adding equations (1) and (3), we have

$\begin{array}{c}\underline{\begin{array}{c}\begin{array}{c} \\ 2x+y−3z=0\end{array} \\ \text{}x-y+z=0\end{array}} \\ \text{} 3x−2z=0\end{array}$

We then solve the resulting equation for $z.$ 

$\begin{array}{c}3x−2z=0 \\ \text{}z=\frac{3}{2}x\end{array}$

We back-substitute the expression for $z$ 
into one of the equations and solve for $y.$ 

$\begin{array}{c}2x+y-3(\frac{3}{2}x)=0 \\ 2x+y-\frac{9}{2}x=0 \\ \text{}y=\frac{9}{2}x-2x \\ \text{}y=\frac{5}{2}x\end{array}$

So the general solution is $(x,\frac{5}{2}x,\frac{3}{2}x).$ 
In this solution, $x$ 
can be any real number. The values of $y$ 
and $z$ 
are dependent on the value selected for $x.$

questions.prompt: 49 . Derive $R=\frac{v_{0}^{2} \text{sin} (2θ)_{0}}{g}$ for the range of a projectile on level ground by finding the time $t$ at which $y$ becomes zero and substituting this value of $t$ into the expression for $x-x_{0}$ , noting that $R=x-x_{0}$
hints: Decompose into x and y components, apply kinematic equations to each.
Apply the relevant law or formula step by step. Check units.
The answer is $R = \frac{(v_{0})^{2} \text{sin} 2θ}{g}$.
questions.solution:
Answer: $R = \frac{(v_{0})^{2} \text{sin} 2θ}{g}$

$y-y_{0}=0=v_{0y}t-\frac{1}{2}(gt)^{2}=(v_{0} \text{sin} θ)t-\frac{1}{2}(gt)^{2}$ ,

so that $t=\frac{2(v_{0} \text{sin} θ)}{g}$ 

$x-x_{0}=v_{0x}t=(v_{0} \text{cos} θ)t=R,$ and substituting for $t$ gives:

$R=v_{0} \text{cos} θ(\frac{(2v)_{0} \text{sin} θ}{g})=\frac{(2v)_{0}^{2} \text{sin} θ \text{cos} θ}{g}$ 

since $2 \text{sin} θ \text{cos} θ=\text{sin} 2θ,$ the range is:

$R=\frac{(v_{0})^{2} \text{sin} 2θ}{g}$ .

questions.solution:

The inverse function takes an output of $f$ and returns an input for $f.$ So in the expression $f^{-1}(70),$ 70 is an output value of the original function, representing 70 miles. questions.solution:
By definition, an exponential function has a constant as a base and an independent variable as an exponent. Thus, $g(x)=x^{3}$ does not represent an exponential function because the base is an independent variable. In fact, $g(x)=x^{3}$ is a power function.

questions.prompt: Writing an Exponential Model When the Initial Value Is Known In 2006, 80 deer were introduced into a wildlife refuge. By 2012, the population had grown to 180 deer. We let our independent variable $t$ be the number of years after 2006. Thus, the information given in the problem can be written as input-output pairs: (0, 80) and (6, 180). questions.prompt: Calculating Compound Interest If we invest \$3,000 in an investment account paying 3% interest compounded quarterly, how much will the account be worth in 10 years?
hints: Take the log (or natural log) of both sides, then solve the resulting linear equation in the exponent.

Because we are starting with \$3,000, $P=3000.$ Our interest rate is 3%, so $r \text{}= \text{}0.03.$ Because we are compounding quarterly, we are compounding 4 times per year, so $n=4.$ We want to kn…

questions.solution:
Because we are starting with \$3,000, $P=3000.$ Our interest rate is 3%, so $r \text{}= \text{}0.03.$ Because we are compounding quarterly, we are compounding 4 times per year, so $n=4.$ We want to know the value of the account in 10 years, so we are looking for $A(10),$ the value when $t \text{}= \text{}10.$ 

$\begin{array}{cccccc}A(t) & =P(1+\frac{r}{n})^{nt} & \text{Use the compound interest formula}. \\ A(10) & =3000(1+\frac{0.03}{4})^{4⋅10}\begin{array}{cccc} & & & \end{array} & \text{Substitute using given values}. \\ & \approx\text{\$}4045.05 & \text{Round to two decimal places}.\end{array}$

The account will be worth about \$4,045.05 in 10 years.

questions.solution:
When an amount grows at a fixed percent per unit time, the growth is exponential. To find $A_{0}$ we use the fact that $A_{0}$ is the amount at time zero, so $A_{0}=10.$ To find $k,$ use the fact that after one hour $(t=1)$ the population doubles from $10$ to $20.$ The formula is derived as follows

$\begin{array}{cc}20=10e^{k\cdot 1} & \\ 2=e^{k} & \text{Divide by 10} \\ \ln2=k & \text{Take the natural logarithm}\end{array}$

so $k=\ln(2).$ Thus the equation we want to graph is $y=10e^{(\ln2)t}=10(e^{\ln2})^{t}=10\cdot 2^{t}.$ The graph is shown in Figure 5 .

hints: Take the log (or natural log) of both sides, then solve the resulting linear equation in the exponent.
This formula is derived as follows.
The answer is $t,$.
questions.solution:
This formula is derived as follows.

$\begin{array}{cc}A=A_{0}e^{kt} & \text{The continuous growth formula}. \\ 0.5A_{0}=A_{0}e^{k\cdot 5730} & \text{Substitute the half-life for }t \text{and }0.5A_{0} \text{for }f(t). \\ 0.5=e^{5730k} & \text{Divide by }A_{0}. \\ \ln(0.5)=5730k & \text{Take the natural log of both sides}. \\ k=\frac{\ln(0.5)}{5730} & \text{Divide by the coefficient of }k. \\ A=A_{0}e^{(\frac{\ln(0.5)}{5730})t} & \text{Substitute for }r \text{in the continuous growth formula}.\end{array}$

The function that describes this continuous decay is $f(t)=A_{0}e^{(\frac{\ln(0.5)}{5730})t}.$ We observe that the coefficient of $t,$ $\frac{\ln(0.5)}{5730}\approx-1.2097\times \mathrm{10}^{−4}$ is negative, as expected in the case of exponential decay.

questions.prompt: Using Newton’s Law of Cooling A cheesecake is taken out of the oven with an ideal internal temperature of $\text{165°F,}$ and is placed into a $35°F$ refrigerator. After 10 minutes, the cheesecake has cooled to $\text{150°F}\text{.}$ If we must wait until the cheesecake has cooled to $\text{70°F}$ before we eat it, how long will we have to wait?
hints: Take the log (or natural log) of both sides, then solve the resulting linear equation in the exponent.

Because the surrounding air temperature in the refrigerator is 35 degrees, the cheesecake’s temperature will decay exponentially toward 35, following the equation

$T(t)=Ae^{kt}+35$ 
We know the initi…
The answer is $\text{70°F}\text{.}$.
questions.solution:
Because the surrounding air temperature in the refrigerator is 35 degrees, the cheesecake’s temperature will decay exponentially toward 35, following the equation

$T(t)=Ae^{kt}+35$ 
We know the initial temperature was 165, so $T(0)=165.$ 

$\begin{array}{cc}165=Ae^{k0}+35 & \text{Substitute }(0,165). \\ A=130 & \text{Solve for }A.\end{array}$

We were given another data point, $T(10)=150,$ which we can use to solve for $k.$ 
$\begin{array}{cc}150=130e^{k10}+35 & \text{Substitute (10, 150)}. \\ 115=130e^{k10} & \text{Subtract 35}. \\ \frac{115}{130}=e^{10k} & \text{Divide by 130}. \\ \ln(\frac{115}{130})=10k & \text{Take the natural log of both sides}. \\ k=\frac{\ln(\frac{115}{130})}{10}\approx-0.0123 & \text{Divide by the coefficient of }k.\end{array}$

This gives us the equation for the cooling of the cheesecake: $T(t)=130e^{–0.0123t}+35.$ 

Now we can solve for the time it will take for the temperature to cool to 70 degrees.
$\begin{array}{cc}70=130e^{-0.0123t}+35 & \text{Substitute in 70 for }T(t). \\ 35=130e^{-0.0123t} & \text{Subtract 35}. \\ \frac{35}{130}=e^{-0.0123t} & \text{Divide by 130}. \\ \ln(\frac{35}{130})=-0.0123t & \text{Take the natural log of both sides} \\ t=\frac{\ln(\frac{35}{130})}{-0.0123}\approx106.68 & \text{Divide by the coefficient of }t.\end{array}$

It will take about 107 minutes, or one hour and 47 minutes, for the cheesecake to cool to $\text{70°F}\text{.}$

If we draw a line between any two of the points, most or all of the points between those two points lie above the line, so the graph is concave down, suggesting a logarithmic model. We can try $y=a\ln(bx).$ Plugging in the first point, $(\text{1,0})\text{,}$ gives $0=a\lnb.$ We reject the case that $a=0$ (if it were, all outputs would be 0), so we know $\ln(b)=0.$ Thus $b=1$ and $y=a\ln(\text{x}).$ Next we can use the point $(\text{9,4}\text{.394})$ to solve for $a:$ 

$\begin{array}{c}y=a\ln(x) \\ 4.394=a\ln(9) \\ a=\frac{4.394}{\ln(9)}\end{array}$

Because $a=\frac{4.394}{\ln(9)}\approx2,$ an appropriate model for the data is $y=2\ln(x).$

questions.solution:
We begin by writing the problem as a fraction.

$\frac{(2+5i)}{(4-i)}$ 

Then we multiply the numerator and denominator by the complex conjugate of the denominator.

$\frac{(2+5i)}{(4-i)} \cdot \frac{(4+i)}{(4+i)}$ 

To multiply two complex numbers, we expand the product as we would with polynomials (using FOIL).

$\begin{array}{cccc}\frac{(2+5i)}{(4-i)}\cdot \frac{(4+i)}{(4+i)} & = & \frac{8+2i+20i+5i^{2}}{16+4i-4i-i^{2}} & \\ & = & \frac{8+2i+20i+5(−1)}{16+4i-4i-(−1)} & \text{Because}i^{2}=−1. \\ & = & \frac{3+22i}{17} & \\ & = & \frac{3}{17}+\frac{22}{17}i & \text{Separate real and imaginary parts}.\end{array}$

Note that this expresses the quotient in standard form.

questions.prompt: Find Coordinates Find the coordinates of the point on the unit circle at an angle of $\frac{7π}{6}.$
hints: Reduce to a reference angle, then use unit-circle values and the sign from the relevant quadrant.
We know that the angle $\frac{7π}{6}$ is in the third quadrant.
The answer is $(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2},-\frac{1}{2})$.
questions.solution:
We know that the angle $\frac{7π}{6}$ is in the third quadrant. 

First, let’s find the reference angle by measuring the angle to the x -axis. To find the reference angle of an angle whose terminal side is in quadrant III, we find the difference of the angle and $π.$ 

$\frac{7π}{6}-π=\frac{π}{6}$

Next, we will find the cosine and sine of the reference angle:

$\cos(\frac{π}{6})=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \sin(\frac{π}{6})=\frac{1}{2}$

We must determine the appropriate signs for x and y in the given quadrant. Because our original angle is in the third quadrant, where both $x$ and $y$ are negative, both cosine and sine are negative.

$\begin{array}{c}\cos(\frac{7π}{6})=-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ \sin(\frac{7π}{6})=-\frac{1}{2}\end{array}$

Now we can calculate the $(x,y)$ coordinates using the identities $x=\cos θ$ and $y=\sin θ.$ 

The coordinates of the point are $(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2},-\frac{1}{2})$ on the unit circle.

We can simplify this by rewriting both functions in terms of sine and cosine.

$\begin{array}{cc}\frac{\sec t}{\tan t}=\frac{\frac{1}{\cos t}}{\frac{\sin t}{\cos t}} & \text{To divide the functions, we multiply by the reciprocal}. \\ =\frac{1}{\cos t}\frac{\cos t}{\sin t} & \text{Divide out the cosines}. \\ =\frac{1}{\sin t} & \text{Simplify and use the identity}. \\ =\csc t & \end{array}$

By showing that $\frac{\sec t}{\tan t}$ can be simplified to $\csc t,$ we have, in fact, established a new identity.

$\frac{\sec t}{\tan t}=\csc t$

questions.prompt: Finding the Inverse of a Quadratic Function When the Restriction Is Not Specified Restrict the domain and then find the inverse of $f(x)=(x-2)^{2}-3.$

questions.solution:
We can see this is a parabola with vertex at $(2,–3)$ that opens upward. Because the graph will be decreasing on one side of the vertex and increasing on the other side, we can restrict this function to a domain on which it will be one-to-one by limiting the domain to $x\ge2.$ 

To find the inverse, we will use the vertex form of the quadratic. We start by replacing $f(x)$ with a simple variable, $y,$ then solve for $x.$ 

$\begin{array}{cccc}y & = & (x-2)^{2}-3 & \text{  }\text{Interchange }x \text{and }y. \\ x & = & (y-2)^{2}-3 & \text{  }\text{Add 3 to both sides}. \\ x+3 & = & (y-2)^{2} & \text{  }\text{Take the square root}. \\ \pm\sqrt{x+3} & = & y-2 & \text{  }\text{Add 2 to both sides}. \\ 2\pm\sqrt{x+3} & = & y & \text{  }\text{Rename the function}. \\ f^{-1}(x) & = & 2\pm\sqrt{x+3} & \end{array}$

Now we need to determine which case to use. Because we restricted our original function to a domain of $x\ge2,$ the outputs of the inverse should be the same, telling us to utilize the + case

$f^{-1}(x)=2+\sqrt{x+3}$

If the quadratic had not been given in vertex form, rewriting it into vertex form would be the first step. This way we may easily observe the coordinates of the vertex to help us restrict the domain.

questions.prompt: Using Polynomial Division in an Application Problem The volume of a rectangular solid is given by the polynomial $3x^{4}-3x^{3}-33x^{2}+54x.$ The length of the solid is given by $3x$ and the width is given by $x-2.$ Find the height, $h,$ of the solid.

questions.solution:

$\begin{array}{ccc}V & = & l\cdot w\cdot h \\ 3x^{4}-3x^{3}-33x^{2}+54x & = & 3x\cdot (x-2)\cdot h\end{array}$ 

To solve for $h,$ first divide both sides by $3x.$ 

$\begin{array}{ccc}\frac{3x\cdot (x-2)\cdot h}{3x} & = & \frac{3x^{4}-3x^{3}-33x^{2}+54x}{3x} \\ (x-2)h & = & x^{3}-x^{2}-11x+18\end{array}$

questions.solution:

The constant term is –4; the factors of –4 are $p=±1,±2,±4.$ 

The leading coefficient is 2; the factors of 2 are $q=±1,±2.$ 

If any of the four real zeros are rational zeros, then they will be of one of the following factors of –4 divided by one of the factors of 2.

$\begin{array}{ccc}\frac{p}{q}=\pm \frac{1}{1}, \pm \frac{1}{2} \text{   } & \frac{p}{q}=\pm \frac{2}{1},\pm \frac{2}{2} \text{   } & \frac{p}{q}= \pm \frac{4}{1},\pm \frac{4}{2}\end{array}$

questions.prompt: Find Rational Zeros Use the Rational Zero Theorem to find the rational zeros of $f(x)=2x^{3}+x^{2}-4x+1.$
hints: Set up long division (or synthetic division if the divisor is $x - c$). Bring down each term in order.

The Rational Zero Theorem tells us that if $\frac{p}{q}$ is a zero of $f(x),$ 
then $p$ is a factor of 1 and $q$ is a factor of 2.
The answer is $f(x).$.
questions.solution:
The Rational Zero Theorem tells us that if $\frac{p}{q}$ is a zero of $f(x),$ 
then $p$ is a factor of 1 and $q$ is a factor of 2. 

$\begin{array}{ccc}\frac{p}{q} & = & \frac{\text{factor of constant term}}{\text{factor of leading coefficient}} \\ & = & \frac{\text{factor of 1}}{\text{factor of 2}}\end{array}$

The factors of 1 are $±1$ and the factors of 2 are $±1$ and $±2.$ The possible values for $\frac{p}{q}$ are $±1$ and $\pm\frac{1}{2}.$ These are the possible rational zeros for the function. We can determine which of the possible zeros are actual zeros by substituting these values for $x$ in $f(x).$ 

$\begin{array}{ccc}f(−1) & = & 2(−1)^{3}+(−1)^{2}-4(−1)+1=4 \\ f(1) & = & 2(1)^{3}+(1)^{2}-4(1)+1=0 \\ f(-\frac{1}{2}) & = & 2(-\frac{1}{2})^{3}+(-\frac{1}{2})^{2}-4(-\frac{1}{2})+1=3 \\ f(\frac{1}{2}) & = & 2(\frac{1}{2})^{3}+(\frac{1}{2})^{2}-4(\frac{1}{2})+1=-\frac{1}{2}\end{array}$

Of those, $−1,-\frac{1}{2}, \text{and }\frac{1}{2}$ are not zeros of $f(x).$ 1 is the only rational zero of $f(x).$

These are the possible rational zeros for the function. We will use synthetic division to evaluate each possible zero until we find one that gives a remainder of 0. Let’s begin with 1.

Because $x=i$

is also a zero. The polynomial must have factors of $(x+3), (x-2), (x-i),$ and $(x+i).$ Since we are looking for a degree 4 polynomial, and now have four zeros, we have all four factors. Let’s begin by multiplying these factors.

$\begin{array}{ccc}f(x) & = & a(x+3)(x-2)(x-i)(x+i) \\ f(x) & = & a(x^{2}+x-6)(x^{2}+1) \\ f(x) & = & a(x^{4}+x^{3}-5x^{2}+x-6)\end{array}$ 
We need to find a to ensure $f(–2)=100.$ Substitute $x=–2$ and $f(2)=100$

$\begin{array}{ccc}100 & = & a((−2)^{4}+(−2)^{3}-5(−2)^{2}+(−2)-6) \\ 100 & = & a(−20) \\ −5 & = & a\end{array}$

questions.prompt: The bakery wants the volume of a small sheet cake to be 351 cubic inches. The cake is in the shape of a rectangular solid. They want the length of the cake to be four inches longer than the width of the cake and the height of the cake to be one-third of the width. What should the dimensions of the cake pan be?
hints: Set up long division (or synthetic division if the divisor is $x - c$). Bring down each term in order.
Begin by writing an equation for the volume of the cake.
The answer is $x = 9$.
questions.solution:
Begin by writing an equation for the volume of the cake. The volume of a rectangular solid is given by $V=lwh.$ We were given that the length must be four inches longer than the width, so we can express the length of the cake as $l=w+4.$ We were given that the height of the cake is one-third of the width, so we can express the height of the cake as $h=\frac{1}{3}w.$ Let’s write the volume of the cake in terms of width of the cake.

$\begin{array}{ccc}V & = & (w+4)(w)(\frac{1}{3}w) \\ V & = & \frac{1}{3}w^{3}+\frac{4}{3}w^{2}\end{array}$

Substitute the given volume into this equation.

$\begin{array}{cccc}351 & = & \frac{1}{3}w^{3}+\frac{4}{3}w^{2} & \text{Substitute 351 for }V. \\ 1053 & = & w^{3}+4w^{2} & \text{Multiply both sides by 3}. \\ 0 & = & w^{3}+4w^{2}-1053 & \text{Subtract 1053 from both sides}.\end{array}$

Descartes' rule of signs tells us there is one positive solution. The Rational Zero Theorem tells us that the possible rational zeros are $\pm1, \pm3, \pm9, \pm13, \pm27, \pm39, \pm81, \pm117, \pm351,$ 
and $\pm1053.$ 
We can use synthetic division to test these possible zeros. Only positive numbers make sense as dimensions for a cake, so we need not test any negative values. Let’s begin by testing values that make the most sense as dimensions for a small sheet cake. Use synthetic division to check $x=1.$ 

Since 1 is not a solution, we will check $x=3.$ 

Since 3 is not a solution either, we will test $x=9.$ 

Synthetic division gives a remainder of 0, so 9 is a solution to the equation. We can use the relationships between the width and the other dimensions to determine the length and height of the sheet cake pan.

$l=w+4=9+4=13 \text{and }h=\frac{1}{3}w=\frac{1}{3}(9)=3$ 

The sheet cake pan should have dimensions 13 inches by 9 inches by 3 inches.

questions.prompt: Identifying Horizontal Asymptotes In the sugar concentration problem earlier, we created the equation $C(t)=\frac{5+t}{100+10t}.$ Find the horizontal asymptote and interpret it in context of the problem.

questions.solution:
Both the numerator and denominator are linear (degree 1). Because the degrees are equal, there will be a horizontal asymptote at the ratio of the leading coefficients. questions.prompt: 131 . [T] Suppose that $a_{1}=S_{1}=1$ and that, for given numbers $S\gt 1$ and $0\lt k\lt 1,$ one defines $a_{n+1}=k(S-S_{n})$ and $S_{n+1}=a_{n+1}+S_{n}.$ Does $S_{n}$ converge? If so, to what? ( Hint: First argue that $S_{n}\lt S$ for all $n$ and $S_{n}$ is increasing.)
hints: Identify arithmetic (constant difference) or geometric (constant ratio), then use the explicit formula.
Apply the rule step by step and double-check each operation.
The answer is $S_{n}\toS.$.
questions.solution:
Answer: $S_{n}\toS.$

Since $S\gt 1,$ $a_{2}\gt 0,$ and since $k\lt 1,$ $S_{2}=1+a_{2}\lt 1+(S-1)=S.$ If $S_{n}\gt S$ for some n , then there is a smallest n . For this n , $S\gt S_{n-1},$ so $S_{n}=S_{n-1}+k(S-S_{n-1})$ $=kS+(1-k)S_{n-1}\lt S,$ a contradiction. Thus $S_{n}\lt S$ and $a_{n+1}\gt 0$ for all n , so $S_{n}$ is increasing and bounded by $S.$ Let $S_{\text{∗}}=\text{lim} S_{n}.$ If $S_{\text{∗}}\lt S,$ then $δ=k(S-S_{\text{∗}})\gt 0,$ but we can find n such that $S_{*}-S_{n}\lt δ\text{/}2,$ which implies that $S_{n+1}=S_{n}+k(S-S_{n})$ $\gt S_{*}+δ\text{/}2,$ contradicting that $S_{n}$ is increasing to $S_{\text{∗}}.$ Thus $S_{n}\toS.$

questions.prompt: 373 . For which values of $r\gt 0,$ if any, does $\sum_{n=1}^{∞}r^{\sqrt{n}}$ converge? ( Hint: $\sum_{n=1}^{∞}a_{n}=\sum_{k=1}^{∞}\sum_{n=k^{2}}^{(k+1)^{2}-1}a_{n}.)$
hints: Identify arithmetic (constant difference) or geometric (constant ratio), then use the explicit formula.
Apply the rule step by step and double-check each operation.
The answer is $r\ge1$.
questions.solution:
Answer: $r\ge1$

$0\lt r\lt 1.$ Note that the ratio and root tests are inconclusive. Using the hint, there are $2k$ terms $r^{\sqrt{n}}$ for $k^{2}\len\lt (k+1)^{2},$ and for $r\lt 1$ each term is at least $r^{k}.$ Thus, $\sum_{n=1}^{∞}r^{\sqrt{n}}=\sum_{k=1}^{∞}\sum_{n=k^{2}}^{(k+1)^{2}-1}r^{\sqrt{n}}$ $\ge\sum_{k=1}^{∞}2kr^{k},$ which converges by the ratio test for $r\lt 1.$ For $r\ge1$ the series diverges by the divergence test.

The answer is $0,π,\frac{7π}{6},\frac{11π}{6}.$.
questions.solution:
This problem should appear familiar as it is similar to a quadratic. Let $\sin θ=x.$ The equation becomes $2x^{2}+x=0.$ We begin by factoring:

$\begin{array}{c}\text{   }2x^{2}+x=0 \\ x(2x+1)=0\end{array}$

Set each factor equal to zero.

$\begin{array}{c}\text{           }x=0\text{  } \\ (2x+1)=0 \\ \text{           }x=-\frac{1}{2}\end{array}$

Then, substitute back into the equation the original expression $\sinθ$ for $x.$ Thus,

$\begin{array}{c}\sin θ=0 \\ \text{     }θ=0,π \\ \\ \sin θ=-\frac{1}{2} \\ \text{     }θ=\frac{7π}{6},\frac{11π}{6}\end{array}$

The solutions within the domain $0\leθ\lt 2π$ are $0,π,\frac{7π}{6},\frac{11π}{6}.$ 

If we prefer not to substitute, we can solve the equation by following the same pattern of factoring and setting each factor equal to zero.

$\begin{array}{c}\text{  }2 \sin^{2}θ+\sin θ=0 \\ \sin θ(2\sin θ+1)=0 \\ \text{                  }\sin θ=0 \\ \text{                       }θ=0,π \\ \\ \text{         }2 \sin θ+1=0 \\ \text{                }2\sin θ=-1 \\ \text{                  }\sin θ=-\frac{1}{2} \\ \text{                       }θ=\frac{7π}{6},\frac{11π}{6}\end{array}$

Notice that the left side of the equation is the difference formula for cosine.

$\begin{array}{ccccc} & \\ \cos x \cos(2x)+\sin x \sin(2x)=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} & \\ \text{                       }\cos(x-2x)=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\begin{array}{cccc} & & & \end{array} & \text{Difference formula for cosine} \\ \text{                           }\cos(−x)=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} & \text{Use the negative angle identity}. \\ \text{                                  }\cos x=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} & \end{array}$

From the unit circle in Figure 2 , we see that $\cos x=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ when $x=\frac{π}{6},\frac{11π}{6}.$

questions.prompt: 53 . Explain why, if $f(a)\ge0$ and f is increasing on $[a,b],$ that the left endpoint estimate is a lower bound for the area below the graph of f on $[a,b].$
hints: Reverse the power rule: increase the exponent by 1 and divide. Add $+ C$.
Apply the rule step by step and double-check each operation.
The answer is $[a,b].$.
questions.solution:
Answer: $[a,b].$

If $[c,d]$ is a subinterval of $[a,b]$ under one of the left-endpoint sum rectangles, then the area of the rectangle contributing to the left-endpoint estimate is $f(c)(d-c).$ But, $f(c)\lef(x)$ for $c\lex\led,$ so the area under the graph of f between c and d is $f(c)(d-c)$ plus the area below the graph of f but above the horizontal line segment at height $f(c),$ which is positive. As this is true for each left-endpoint sum interval, it follows that the left Riemann sum is less than or equal to the area below the graph of f on $[a,b].$

hints: Reverse the power rule: increase the exponent by 1 and divide. Add $+ C$.
Apply the rule step by step and double-check each operation.
The answer is $b-a$.
questions.solution:
Answer: $b-a$

The integral of f over an interval is the same as the integral of the average of f over that interval. Thus, $\begin{array}{c}\int_{a}^{b}f(t)dt=\int_{a_{0}}^{a_{1}}f(t)dt+\int_{a_{1}}^{a_{2}}f(t)dt+\text{⋯}+\int_{a_{N+1}}^{a_{N}}f(t)dt=\int_{a_{0}}^{a_{1}}1dt+\int_{a_{1}}^{a_{2}}1dt+\text{⋯}+\int_{a_{N+1}}^{a_{N}}1dt \\ =(a_{1}-a_{0})+(a_{2}-a_{1})+\text{⋯}+(a_{N}-a_{N-1})=a_{N}-a_{0}=b-a.\end{array}$ Dividing through by $b-a$ gives the desired identity.

questions.prompt: 42 . Calculate the power output needed for a 950-kg car to climb a $2.00º$ slope at a constant 30.0 m/s while encountering wind resistance and friction totaling 600 N. Explicitly show how you follow the steps in the Problem-Solving Strategies for Energy .
hints: Work-energy theorem $W = \Delta KE$. Conservation of energy.
Apply the relevant law or formula step by step. Check units.
The answer is $F = f+w=\text{600 N}+\text{mg} \text{sin} θ$.
questions.solution:
Answer: $F = f+w=\text{600 N}+\text{mg} \text{sin} θ$

Identify knowns: $m=\text{950 kg}$ , $\text{slope angle} θ=2.00º$ ,
$v=3.00 m/s$ , $f=\text{600 N}$ 

Identify unknowns: power $P$ of the car, force $F$ that car applies to road

Solve for unknown: 

$P=\frac{W}{t}=\frac{\text{Fd}}{t}=F(\frac{d}{t})=\text{Fv},$ 

where $F$ is parallel to the incline and must oppose the resistive forces and the force of gravity: 

$F=f+w=\text{600 N}+\text{mg} \text{sin} θ$ 

Insert this into the expression for power and solve:

$\begin{array}{ccc}P & = & (f+\text{mg} \text{sin} θ)v \\ & = & [\text{600 N}+(\text{950 kg})(\text{9.80 m/s}^{2})\text{sin 2º}](\text{30.0 m/s}) \\ & = & \text{2.77}\times \text{10}^{4} W\end{array}$ 

About 28 kW (or about 37 hp) is reasonable for a car to climb a gentle incline.

questions.prompt: 57 . Derive the equation for the vertical acceleration of a rocket.
hints: Momentum $p = mv$ is conserved. Use elastic vs inelastic conditions.
Apply the relevant law or formula step by step. Check units.
The answer is $m$.
questions.solution:
Answer: $m$

The force needed to give a small mass $\text{Δ}m$ an acceleration $a_{\text{Δ}m}$ is $F=\text{Δ}\text{ma}_{\text{Δ}m}$ . To accelerate this mass in the small time interval $\text{Δ}t$ requires $v_{\text{e}}=a_{\text{Δ}m}\text{Δ}t$ , so $F=v_{\text{e}}\frac{\text{Δ}m}{\text{Δ}t}$ . By Newton’s third law, this force is equal in magnitude to the thrust force acting on the rocket, so $F_{\text{thrust}}=v_{\text{e}}\frac{\text{Δ}m}{\text{Δ}t}$ , where all quantities are positive. Applying Newton’s second law to the rocket gives $F_{\text{thrust}}-\text{mg}=\text{ma}\Rightarrowa=\frac{v_{\text{e}}}{m}\frac{\text{Δ}m}{\text{Δ}t}-g$ , where $m$ is the mass of the rocket and unburnt fuel.

questions.prompt: 84 . What is the effect on the concentration of acetic acid, hydronium ion, and acetate ion when the following are added to an acidic buffer solution of equal concentrations of acetic acid and sodium acetate: (a) HCl (b) KCH 3 CO 2 (c) NaCl (d) KOH (e) CH 3 CO 2 H

The answer is $[\text{CH}_{3}\text{CO}_{2}^{\text{−}}]$.
questions.solution:
Answer: $[\text{CH}_{3}\text{CO}_{2}^{\text{−}}]$

(a) The added HCl will increase the concentration of H 3 O + slightly, which will react with $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CO}_{2}^{\text{−}}$ and produce CH 3 CO 2 H in the process. Thus, $[\text{CH}_{3}\text{CO}_{2}^{\text{−}}]$ decreases and [CH 3 CO 2 H] increases.
(b) The added KCH 3 CO 2 will increase the concentration of $[\text{CH}_{3}\text{CO}_{2}^{\text{−}}]$ which will react with H 3 O + and produce CH 3 CO 2 H in the process. Thus, [H 3 O + ] decreases slightly and [CH 3 CO 2 H] increases.
(c) The added NaCl will have no effect on the concentration of the ions.
(d) The added KOH will produce OH − ions, which will react with the H 3 O + , thus reducing [H 3 O + ]. Some additional CH 3 CO 2 H will dissociate, producing $[\text{CH}_{3}\text{CO}_{2}^{\text{−}}]$ ions in the process. Thus, [CH 3 CO 2 H] decreases slightly and $[\text{CH}_{3}\text{CO}_{2}^{\text{−}}]$ increases.
(e) The added CH 3 CO 2 H will increase its concentration, causing more of it to dissociate and producing more $[\text{CH}_{3}\text{CO}_{2}^{\text{−}}]$ and H 3 O + in the process. Thus, [H 3 O + ] increases slightly and $[\text{CH}_{3}\text{CO}_{2}^{\text{−}}]$ increases.

questions.solution:
First, we write this as an augmented matrix.

$[\begin{array}{cc}2 & 3 \\ 1 & −1\end{array} \text{ }| \text{ }\begin{array}{c}6 \\ \frac{1}{2}\end{array}]$

We want a 1 in row 1, column 1. This can be accomplished by interchanging row 1 and row 2.

$R_{1}↔R_{2}\to[\begin{array}{ccc}1 & −1 & \\ 2 & 3 & \end{array}|\begin{array}{cc} & \frac{1}{2} \\ & 6\end{array}]$

We now have a 1 as the first entry in row 1, column 1. Now let’s obtain a 0 in row 2, column 1. This can be accomplished by multiplying row 1 by $−2,$ and then adding the result to row 2.
$−2R_{1}+R_{2}=R_{2}\to[\begin{array}{ccc}1 & −1 & \\ 0 & 5 & \end{array}|\begin{array}{cc} & \frac{1}{2} \\ & 5\end{array}]$

We only have one more step, to multiply row 2 by $\frac{1}{5}.$ 

$\frac{1}{5}R_{2}=R_{2}\to[\begin{array}{ccc}1 & −1 & \\ 0 & 1 & \end{array}|\begin{array}{cc} & \frac{1}{2} \\ & 1\end{array}]$

Use back-substitution. The second row of the matrix represents $y=1.$ Back-substitute $y=1$ into the first equation.

$\begin{array}{c}x-(1)=\frac{1}{2} \\ \text{        }x=\frac{3}{2}\end{array}$

The solution is the point $(\frac{3}{2},1).$

questions.solution:
Write the system as an augmented matrix .

$[\begin{array}{cc}2 & 1 \\ 4 & 2\end{array} \text{ }| \text{ }\begin{array}{c}1 \\ 6\end{array}]$

Obtain a 1 in row 1, column 1. This can be accomplished by multiplying the first row by $\frac{1}{2}.$ 

$\frac{1}{2}R_{1}=R_{1}\to[\begin{array}{cc}1 & \frac{1}{2} \\ 4 & 2\end{array} \text{ }| \text{ }\begin{array}{c}\frac{1}{2} \\ 6\end{array}]$

Next, we want a 0 in row 2, column 1. Multiply row 1 by $−4$ and add row 1 to row 2.
$−4R_{1}+R_{2}=R_{2}\to[\begin{array}{cc}1 & \frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & 0\end{array} \text{ }| \text{ }\begin{array}{c}\frac{1}{2} \\ 4\end{array}]$

The second row represents the equation $0=4.$ Therefore, the system is inconsistent and has no solution.

$A=[\begin{array}{cccc}3 & & 4 & \\ 6 & & 8 & \end{array}|\begin{array}{cc} & 12 \\ & 24\end{array}]$
$\begin{array}{ccccccccccccccccc} \\ \begin{array}{ccccccccc}-\frac{1}{2}R_{2}+R_{1}=R_{1}\to[\begin{array}{cccc}0 & & 0 & \\ 6 & & 8 & \end{array}|\begin{array}{cc} & 0 \\ & 24\end{array}] \\ R_{1}↔R_{2}\to[\begin{array}{cccc}6 & & 8 & \\ 0 & & 0 & \end{array}|\begin{array}{cc} & 24 \\ & 0\end{array}]\end{array}\end{array}$

The matrix ends up with all zeros in the last row: $0y=0.$ Thus, there are an infinite number of solutions and the system is classified as dependent. To find the generic solution, return to one of the original equations and solve for $y.$ 

$\begin{array}{c}3x+4y=12 \\ \text{        }4y=12−3x \\ \text{          }y=3-\frac{3}{4}x\end{array}$

So the solution to this system is $(x,3-\frac{3}{4}x).$

hints: Match dimensions: an $m \times n$ times an $n \times p$ gives an $m \times p$. Multiply rows by columns.
First, we write the augmented matrix.
The answer is $(4,−3,1).$.
questions.solution:
First, we write the augmented matrix.

$[\begin{array}{ccc}1 & -1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 & -1 \\ 3 & -2 & -9\end{array} \text{  }| \text{ }\begin{array}{c}8 \\ -2 \\ 9\end{array}]$

Next, we perform row operations to obtain row-echelon form.

$\begin{array}{ccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccc}-2R_{1}+R_{2}=R_{2}\to[\begin{array}{cccccc}1 & & -1 & & 1 & \\ 0 & & 5 & & -3 & \\ 3 & & -2 & & -9 & \end{array}|\begin{array}{cc} & 8 \\ & -18 \\ & 9\end{array}] & & & & -3R_{1}+R_{3}=R_{3}\to[\begin{array}{cccccc}1 & & -1 & & 1 & \\ 0 & & 5 & & -3 & \\ 0 & & 1 & & -12 & \end{array}|\begin{array}{cc} & 8 \\ & -18 \\ & -15\end{array}]\end{array}$

The easiest way to obtain a 1 in row 2, column 2 is to interchange $R_{2}$ and $R_{3}.$ 

$\text{Interchange} R_{2} \text{and} R_{3}\to[\begin{array}{ccccccc}1 & & −1 & & 1 & & 8 \\ 0 & & 1 & & −12 & & −15 \\ 0 & & 5 & & −3 & & −18\end{array}]$

Then

$\begin{array}{ccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccc} \\ \begin{array}{ccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccc}−5R_{2}+R_{3}=R_{3}\to[\begin{array}{cccccc}1 & & −1 & & 1 & \\ 0 & & 1 & & −12 & \\ 0 & & 0 & & 57 & \end{array}|\begin{array}{cc} & 8 \\ & −15 \\ & 57\end{array}] & & & & -\frac{1}{57}R_{3}=R_{3}\to[\begin{array}{cccccc}1 & & −1 & & 1 & \\ 0 & & 1 & & −12 & \\ 0 & & 0 & & 1 & \end{array}|\begin{array}{cc} & 8 \\ & −15 \\ & 1\end{array}]\end{array}\end{array}$

The last matrix represents the equivalent system.

$\begin{array}{c}\text{}x-y+z=8 \\ \text{  }y-12z=−15 \\ \text{            }z=1\end{array}$

Using back-substitution, we obtain the solution as $(4,−3,1).$

hints: Match dimensions: an $m \times n$ times an $n \times p$ gives an $m \times p$. Multiply rows by columns.
Write the augmented matrix.
The answer is $(x,\frac{2−2x}{3},\frac{1-x}{3}).$.
questions.solution:
Write the augmented matrix.

$[\begin{array}{ccc}−1 & −2 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & −2\end{array} \text{ }| \text{ }\begin{array}{c}−1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{array}]$

First, multiply row 1 by $−1$ to get a 1 in row 1, column 1. Then, perform row operations to obtain row-echelon form.
$-R_{1}\to[\begin{array}{ccc}1 & 2 & −1 \\ 2 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & −2\end{array} \text{ }| \text{ }\begin{array}{c}1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{array}]$
$R_{2}↔R_{3}\to[\begin{array}{ccccc}1 & & 2 & & -1 \\ 0 & & 1 & & -2 \\ 2 & & 3 & & 0\end{array} \text{ }|\begin{array}{cc} & 1 \\ & 0 \\ & 2\end{array}]$
$−2R_{1}+R_{3}=R_{3}\to[\begin{array}{cccccc}1 & & 2 & & −1 & \\ 0 & & 1 & & −2 & \\ 0 & & −1 & & 2 & \end{array}|\begin{array}{cc} & 1 \\ & 0 \\ & 0\end{array}]$
$R_{2}+R_{3}=R_{3}\to[\begin{array}{cccccc}1 & & 2 & & −1 & \\ 0 & & 1 & & −2 & \\ 0 & & 0 & & 0 & \end{array}|\begin{array}{cc} & 1 \\ & 1 \\ & 0\end{array}]$

The last matrix represents the following system.

$\begin{array}{c}\text{}x+2y-z=1 \\ \text{       }y-2z=0 \\ \text{              }0=0\end{array}$

We see by the identity $0=0$ that this is a dependent system with an infinite number of solutions. We then find the generic solution. By solving the second equation for $y$ and substituting it into the first equation we can solve for $z$ in terms of $x.$ 

$\begin{array}{c}x+2y-z=1 \\ \text{                 }y=2z \\ \\ x+2(2z)-z=1 \\ \text{          }x+3z=1 \\ \text{                 }z=\frac{1-x}{3}\end{array}$

Now we substitute the expression for $z$ into the second equation to solve for $y$ in terms of $x.$ 
$\begin{array}{c}y-2z=0 \\ z=\frac{1-x}{3} \\ \\ y-2(\frac{1-x}{3})=0 \\ y=\frac{2-2x}{3}\end{array}$

The generic solution is $(x,\frac{2−2x}{3},\frac{1-x}{3}).$

questions.prompt: Applying 2 × 2 Matrices to Finance Carolyn invests a total of \$12,000 in two municipal bonds, one paying 10.5% interest and the other paying 12% interest. The annual interest earned on the two investments last year was \$1,335. How much was invested at each rate?
hints: Match dimensions: an $m \times n$ times an $n \times p$ gives an $m \times p$. Multiply rows by columns.
We have a system of two equations in two variables.
The answer is $5,000 was invested at 12% interest and \$.
questions.solution:
We have a system of two equations in two variables. Let $x=$ the amount invested at 10.5% interest, and $y=$ the amount invested at 12% interest.

$\begin{array}{c}\text{               }x+y=12,000 \\ 0.105x+0.12y=1,335\end{array}$

As a matrix, we have

$[\begin{array}{cc}1 & 1 \\ 0.105 & 0.12\end{array} \text{ }| \text{ }\begin{array}{c}12,000 \\ 1,335\end{array}]$

Multiply row 1 by $−0.105$ and add the result to row 2.
$[\begin{array}{cc}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0.015\end{array} \text{ }| \text{ }\begin{array}{c}12,000 \\ 75\end{array}]$

Then,

$\begin{array}{c}0.015y=75 \\ \text{        }y=5,000\end{array}$

So $12,000−5,000=7,000.$ 

Thus, \$5,000 was invested at 12% interest and \$7,000 at 10.5% interest.

questions.prompt: Applying 3 × 3 Matrices to Finance Ava invests a total of \$10,000 in three accounts, one paying 5% interest, another paying 8% interest, and the third paying 9% interest. The annual interest earned on the three investments last year was \$770. The amount invested at 9% was twice the amount invested at 5%. How much was invested at each rate?
hints: Match dimensions: an $m \times n$ times an $n \times p$ gives an $m \times p$. Multiply rows by columns.
We have a system of three equations in three variables.
The answer is $3,000 invested at 5% interest, \$.
questions.solution:
We have a system of three equations in three variables. Let $x$ be the amount invested at 5% interest, let $y$ be the amount invested at 8% interest, and let $z$ be the amount invested at 9% interest. Thus,

$\begin{array}{c}\text{                    }x+y+z=10,000 \\ 0.05x+0.08y+0.09z=770 \\ \text{                        }2x-z=0\end{array}$

As a matrix, we have

$[\begin{array}{ccc}1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0.05 & 0.08 & 0.09 \\ 2 & 0 & −1\end{array} \text{ }| \text{ }\begin{array}{c}10,000 \\ 770 \\ 0\end{array}]$

Now, we perform Gaussian elimination to achieve row-echelon form.

$\begin{array}{ccccccccccccccccccc}\begin{array}{ccccccccccccccccccc} \\ −0.05R_{1}+R_{2}=R_{2}\to[\begin{array}{cccccc}1 & & 1 & & 1 & \\ 0 & & 0.03 & & 0.04 & \\ 2 & & 0 & & −1 & \end{array}|\begin{array}{cc} & 10,000 \\ & 270 \\ & 0\end{array}]\end{array} \\ −2R_{1}+R_{3}=R_{3}\to[\begin{array}{cccccc}1 & & 1 & & 1 & \\ 0 & & 0.03 & & 0.04 & \\ 0 & & −2 & & −3 & \end{array}|\begin{array}{cc} & 10,000 \\ & 270 \\ & −20,000\end{array}] \\ \frac{1}{0.03}R_{2}=R_{2}\to[\begin{array}{cccccc}0 & & 1 & & 1 & \\ 0 & & 1 & & \frac{4}{3} & \\ 0 & & −2 & & −3 & \end{array}|\begin{array}{cc} & 10,000 \\ & 9,000 \\ & −20,000\end{array}] \\ 2R_{2}+R_{3}=R_{3}\to[\begin{array}{cccccc}1 & & 1 & & 1 & \\ 0 & & 1 & & \frac{4}{3} & \\ 0 & & 0 & & -\frac{1}{3} & \end{array}|\begin{array}{cc} & 10,000 \\ & 9,000 \\ & −2,000\end{array}]\end{array}$

The third row tells us $-\frac{1}{3}z=−2,000;$ thus $z=6,000.$ 

The second row tells us $y+\frac{4}{3}z=9,000.$ Substituting $z=6,000,$ we get
$\begin{array}{c}y+\frac{4}{3}(6,000)=9,000 \\ y+8,000=9,000 \\ y=1,000\end{array}$

The first row tells us $x+y+z=10,000.$ Substituting $y=1,000$ and $z=6,000,$ we get
$\begin{array}{c}x+1,000+6,000=10,000 \\ \text{                             }x=3,000\end{array}$

The answer is \$3,000 invested at 5% interest, \$1,000 invested at 8%, and \$6,000 invested at 9% interest.

questions.prompt: Showing That the Identity Matrix Acts as a 1 Given matrix A , show that $AI=IA=A.$ $A=[\begin{array}{cc}3 & 4 \\ −2 & 5\end{array}]$
hints: Match dimensions: an $m \times n$ times an $n \times p$ gives an $m \times p$. Multiply rows by columns.
Use matrix multiplication to show that the product of $A$ and the identity is equal to the product of the identity and A.
The answer is $A$.
questions.solution:
Use matrix multiplication to show that the product of $A$ and the identity is equal to the product of the identity and A. 

$AI=[\begin{array}{ccc}3 & & 4 \\ −2 & & 5\end{array}]\begin{array}{c}\end{array}[\begin{array}{ccc}1 & & 0 \\ 0 & & 1\end{array}]=[\begin{array}{cccc}3\cdot 1+4\cdot 0 & & & 3\cdot 0+4\cdot 1 \\ −2\cdot 1+5\cdot 0 & & & −2\cdot 0+5\cdot 1\end{array}]=[\begin{array}{ccc}3 & & 4 \\ −2 & & 5\end{array}]$
$IA=[\begin{array}{ccc}1 & & 0 \\ 0 & & 1\end{array}]\begin{array}{c}\end{array}[\begin{array}{ccc}3 & & 4 \\ −2 & & 5\end{array}]=[\begin{array}{cccc}1\cdot 3+0\cdot (−2) & & & 1\cdot 4+0\cdot 5 \\ 0\cdot 3+1\cdot (−2) & & & 0\cdot 4+1\cdot 5\end{array}]=[\begin{array}{ccc}3 & & 4 \\ −2 & & 5\end{array}]$

questions.prompt: Show that the given matrices are multiplicative inverses of each other. $A=[\begin{array}{ccc}1 & & 5 \\ −2 & & −9\end{array}],B=[\begin{array}{ccc}−9 & & −5 \\ 2 & & 1\end{array}]$
hints: Match dimensions: an $m \times n$ times an $n \times p$ gives an $m \times p$. Multiply rows by columns.
Multiply $AB$ and $BA.$ If both products equal the identity, then the two matrices are inverses of each other.
The answer is $B$.
questions.solution:
Multiply $AB$ and $BA.$ If both products equal the identity, then the two matrices are inverses of each other.

$\begin{array}{ccccccccc}AB=[\begin{array}{ccc}1 & & 5 \\ −2 & & −9\end{array}]\cdot [\begin{array}{ccc}−9 & & −5 \\ 2 & & 1\end{array}] \\ =[\begin{array}{ccc}1(−9)+5(2) & & 1(−5)+5(1) \\ −2(−9)−9(2) & & −2(−5)−9(1)\end{array}] \\ =[\begin{array}{ccc}1 & & 0 \\ 0 & & 1\end{array}]\end{array}$
$\begin{array}{ccccccccc}BA=[\begin{array}{ccc}−9 & & −5 \\ 2 & & 1\end{array}]\cdot [\begin{array}{ccc}1 & & 5 \\ −2 & & −9\end{array}] \\ =[\begin{array}{ccc}−9(1)−5(−2) & & −9(5)−5(−9) \\ 2(1)+1(−2) & & 2(5)+1(−9)\end{array}] \\ =[\begin{array}{ccc}1 & & 0 \\ 0 & & 1\end{array}]\end{array}$

$A$ and $B$ are inverses of each other.

questions.prompt: Use matrix multiplication to find the inverse of the given matrix. $A=[\begin{array}{ccc}1 & & −2 \\ 2 & & −3\end{array}]$
hints: Match dimensions: an $m \times n$ times an $n \times p$ gives an $m \times p$. Multiply rows by columns.
For this method, we multiply $A$ by a matrix containing unknown constants and set it equal to the identity.
The answer is $b.$.
questions.solution:
For this method, we multiply $A$ by a matrix containing unknown constants and set it equal to the identity.

$[\begin{array}{cc}1 & −2 \\ 2 & −3\end{array}] \text{  }[\begin{array}{cc}a & b \\ c & d\end{array}]=[\begin{array}{cc}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{array}]$

Find the product of the two matrices on the left side of the equal sign.

$[\begin{array}{cc}1 & −2 \\ 2 & −3\end{array}] \text{  }[\begin{array}{cc}a & b \\ c & d\end{array}]=[\begin{array}{cc}1a−2c & 1b−2d \\ 2a−3c & 2b−3d\end{array}]$

Next, set up a system of equations with the entry in row 1, column 1 of the new matrix equal to the first entry of the identity, 1. Set the entry in row 2, column 1 of the new matrix equal to the corresponding entry of the identity, which is 0.
$\begin{array}{c}1a−2c=1 \text{   }R_{1} \\ 2a−3c=0 \text{   }R_{2}\end{array}$

Using row operations, multiply and add as follows: $(−2)R_{1}+R_{2}\toR_{2}.$ Add the equations, and solve for $c.$ 

$\begin{array}{c}1a-2c=1 \\ 0+1c=-2 \\ c=-2\end{array}$

Back-substitute to solve for $a.$ 

$\begin{array}{c}a−2(−2)=1 \\ a+4=1 \\ a=−3\end{array}$

Write another system of equations setting the entry in row 1, column 2 of the new matrix equal to the corresponding entry of the identity, 0. Set the entry in row 2, column 2 equal to the corresponding entry of the identity.

$\begin{array}{cc}1b−2d=0 & R_{1} \\ 2b−3d=1 & R_{2}\end{array}$

Using row operations, multiply and add as follows: $(−2)R_{1}+R_{2}=R_{2}.$ Add the two equations and solve for $d.$ 

$\begin{array}{c}1b−2d=0 \\ \frac{0+1d=1}{ d=1} \\ \end{array}$

Once more, back-substitute and solve for $b.$ 

$\begin{array}{c}b−2(1)=0 \\ b−2=0 \\ b=2\end{array}$
$A^{−1}=[\begin{array}{ccc}−3 & & 2 \\ −2 & & 1\end{array}]$

hints: Match dimensions: an $m \times n$ times an $n \times p$ gives an $m \times p$. Multiply rows by columns.
Write the system in terms of a coefficient matrix, a variable matrix, and a constant matrix.
The answer is $(−1,1).$.
questions.solution:
Write the system in terms of a coefficient matrix, a variable matrix, and a constant matrix.

$A=[\begin{array}{cc}3 & 8 \\ 4 & 11\end{array}],X=[\begin{array}{c}x \\ y\end{array}],B=[\begin{array}{c}5 \\ 7\end{array}]$

Then

$[\begin{array}{cc}3 & 8 \\ 4 & 11\end{array}] \text{  }[\begin{array}{c}x \\ y\end{array}]=[\begin{array}{c}5 \\ 7\end{array}]$

First, we need to calculate $A^{−1}.$ Using the formula to calculate the inverse of a 2 by 2 matrix, we have:

$\begin{array}{ccc}A^{−1}=\frac{1}{ad-bc}[\begin{array}{cc}d & -b \\ -c & a\end{array}] \\ \text{     }=\frac{1}{3(11)−8(4)}[\begin{array}{cc}11 & −8 \\ −4 & 3\end{array}] \\ \text{     }=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{array}{cc}11 & −8 \\ −4 & 3\end{array}]\end{array}$

So,

$A^{−1}=[\begin{array}{cc}11 & −8 \\ −4 & \text{​}\text{​} 3\end{array}]$

Now we are ready to solve. Multiply both sides of the equation by $A^{−1}.$ 

$\begin{array}{ccccccc} (A^{−1})AX=(A^{−1})B \\ [\begin{array}{cc}11 & −8 \\ −4 & 3\end{array}] \text{  }[\begin{array}{cc}3 & 8 \\ 4 & 11\end{array}] \text{  }[\begin{array}{c}x \\ y\end{array}]=[\begin{array}{cc}11 & −8 \\ −4 & 3\end{array}] \text{  }[\begin{array}{c}5 \\ 7\end{array}] \\ [\begin{array}{cc}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{array}] \text{  }[\begin{array}{c}x \\ y\end{array}]=[\begin{array}{c}11(5)+(−8)7 \\ −4(5)+3(7)\end{array}] \\ [\begin{array}{c}x \\ y\end{array}]=[\begin{array}{c}−1 \\ 1\end{array}]\end{array}$

The solution is $(−1,1).$

hints: Match dimensions: an $m \times n$ times an $n \times p$ gives an $m \times p$. Multiply rows by columns.

Write the equation $AX=B.$ 

$[\begin{array}{ccc}5 & 15 & 56 \\ −4 & −11 & −41 \\ −1 & −3 & −11\end{array}] \text{  }[\begin{array}{c}x \\ y \\ z\end{array}]=[\begin{array}{c}35 \\ −26 \\ −7\end{array…
The answer is $(1,2,0).$.
questions.solution:
Write the equation $AX=B.$ 

$[\begin{array}{ccc}5 & 15 & 56 \\ −4 & −11 & −41 \\ −1 & −3 & −11\end{array}] \text{  }[\begin{array}{c}x \\ y \\ z\end{array}]=[\begin{array}{c}35 \\ −26 \\ −7\end{array}]$

First, we will find the inverse of $A$ by augmenting with the identity.

$[\begin{array}{ccc}5 & 15 & 56 \\ −4 & −11 & −41 \\ −1 & −3 & −11\end{array} | \begin{array}{ccc}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{array}]$

Multiply row 1 by $\frac{1}{5}.$ 

$[\begin{array}{ccc}1 & 3 & \frac{56}{5} \\ −4 & −11 & −41 \\ −1 & −3 & −11\end{array} | \begin{array}{ccc}\frac{1}{5} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{array}]$

Multiply row 1 by 4 and add to row 2.

$[\begin{array}{ccc}1 & 3 & \frac{56}{5} \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{19}{5} \\ −1 & −3 & −11\end{array} | \begin{array}{ccc}\frac{1}{5} & 0 & 0 \\ \frac{4}{5} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{array}]$

Add row 1 to row 3.

$[\begin{array}{ccc}1 & 3 & \frac{56}{5} \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{19}{5} \\ 0 & 0 & \frac{1}{5}\end{array} | \begin{array}{ccc}\frac{1}{5} & 0 & 0 \\ \frac{4}{5} & 1 & 0 \\ \frac{1}{5} & 0 & 1\end{array}]$

Multiply row 2 by −3 and add to row 1.

$[\begin{array}{ccc}1 & 0 & -\frac{1}{5} \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{19}{5} \\ 0 & 0 & \frac{1}{5}\end{array} | \begin{array}{ccc}-\frac{11}{5} & −3 & 0 \\ \frac{4}{5} & 1 & 0 \\ \frac{1}{5} & 0 & 1\end{array}]$

Multiply row 3 by 5.

$[\begin{array}{ccc}1 & 0 & -\frac{1}{5} \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{19}{5} \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{array} | \begin{array}{ccc}-\frac{11}{5} & −3 & 0 \\ \frac{4}{5} & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 5\end{array}]$

Multiply row 3 by $\frac{1}{5}$ and add to row 1.

$[\begin{array}{ccc}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{19}{5} \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{array} | \begin{array}{ccc}−2 & −3 & 1 \\ \frac{4}{5} & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 5\end{array}]$

Multiply row 3 by $-\frac{19}{5}$ and add to row 2.

$[\begin{array}{ccc}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{array} | \begin{array}{ccc}−2 & −3 & 1 \\ −3 & 1 & −19 \\ 1 & 0 & 5\end{array}]$

So,

$A^{−1}=[\begin{array}{ccc}−2 & −3 & 1 \\ −3 & 1 & −19 \\ 1 & 0 & 5\end{array}]$

Multiply both sides of the equation by $A^{−1}.$ We want $A^{−1}AX=A^{−1}B:$ 

$[\begin{array}{ccc}−2 & −3 & 1 \\ −3 & 1 & −19 \\ 1 & 0 & 5\end{array}] \text{  }[\begin{array}{ccc}5 & 15 & 56 \\ −4 & −11 & −41 \\ −1 & −3 & −11\end{array}] \text{  }[\begin{array}{c}x \\ y \\ z\end{array}]=[\begin{array}{ccc}−2 & −3 & 1 \\ −3 & 1 & −19 \\ 1 & 0 & 5\end{array}] \text{  }[\begin{array}{c}35 \\ −26 \\ −7\end{array}]$

Thus,

$A^{−1}B=[\begin{array}{c}−70+78−7 \\ −105−26+133 \\ 35+0−35\end{array}]=[\begin{array}{c}1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{array}]$

The solution is $(1,2,0).$
